title: Optional trochoidal/whirling engagement overlay on the thread-mill helix (hard-material thread milling)
description: REFRAMED 2026-06-01 (was: 'implement true thread-whirling operation'). The original framing was a category error: it read Estlcam's German 'Wirbeln' label as the LATHE thread-whirling technique and asked for a turning op. But (a) Estlcam 'Wirbeln' is a trochoidal face-mill overlay (gcode/wirbeln.rs -> face_mill_overlay), NOT threading; and (b) true thread-whirling is a lathe technique needing MachineMode::Lathe + rotary kinematics + a turning post — an explicit non-goal. In a MILLING context the need is already served by thread milling (OpKind::Thread / op_drivers/thread.rs): internal/external, climb, radial multi-pass (sqnh), thread forms via thread_depth_mm (mniu), mid-helix resume (6uns), form-aware ThreadMill tool (gm1u). The ONE real milling gap: on hard materials a single full-engagement thread helix overloads the cutting edge. This issue: optionally superimpose the EXISTING trochoidal whirling overlay onto the thread helix to soften per-tooth chipload — 'thread whirling' in the only sense that is buildable on our 3-axis platform.
design: Confirmed: the Thread op emits via emit_vcarve_block (raw point-by-point G1 in gcode.rs) which does NOT route through walk.rs::emit_cut_path, where apply_wirbeln_with_state lives — so a whirling-tagged tool on a Thread op currently has NO effect on the helix (no collision, no hybrid). This feature is purely additive. Two viable implementations: (1) route the Thread helix polyline through the overlay-aware cut walker so the existing WirbelnParams (radius/stepover/osc/climb) apply; or (2) add an orbital component directly in thread.rs helix_waypoints. Prefer reusing wirbeln.rs to avoid a second orbital model. Default OFF = today's behavior (backward compatible).
acceptance_criteria: 1. A way to opt into orbital/trochoidal engagement on a Thread op (per-op flag or via a whirling-tagged ThreadMill tool). 2. The thread helix gains the orbital overlay (route through walk.rs::apply_wirbeln_with_state OR add orbital term in helix_waypoints). 3. Orbit params (radius/stepover/osc) resolved sensibly for thread geometry; guard so orbit radius cannot breach the thread flank (warning if it would). 4. Default off (backward compatible); sim + snapshot coverage. NON-GOAL: lathe thread-whirling (no MachineMode::Lathe).
notes: Terminology lock: 'Wirbeln'/'whirling' in this codebase = trochoidal milling overlay (face_mill_overlay), NEVER threading. Keep distinct in UI. True lathe thread-whirling stays out of scope until/unless a turning platform is scoped.
close_reason: Shipped: whirl-tagged ThreadMill superimposes the orbit on the helix via apply_whirl_to_polyline (phase-continuous across passes), quarter-pitch flank clamp + warning, osc forced off, lead-in plain, default off. Tests pin densification, no-warn in-cap, and the clamp warning. 823 core tests + clippy green.

title: toolchange envelope: spindle_cw uses tool.speed (rough) not finish-pass speed
description: emit_toolchange_envelope (pipeline.rs) calls post.spindle_cw(t.speed, 0) at the end of the M6 envelope, where t is the ToolEntry. For a tool with speed_finish set (different from speed), this emits M3 at the rough RPM, then the next emit_polylines_block re-emits M3 at the finish RPM via the delta-encoder. Functionally correct (the final speed is right by the cut) but emits a redundant transient M3 line. Plumb the target speed as a parameter to the helper so callers (dual_tool, drill_stufenfase) can pass speed_finish directly. Low-priority cosmetic — affects gcode size, not correctness.
close_reason: Fixed and committed on main; full wiac-core + wiac-wasm test suites green, clippy clean. mg77: catch_unwind guard on sim advance/partial_advance. n3hn: clamp vcarve pre-polyline plunge to max(start_depth, entry_z). liyy: target_speed param so finish-pass toolchange envelope spins up at finish RPM.

title: vcarve: make lead-in ramp angle configurable per-tool
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/cam/vcarve_emit.rs (the `LEAD_IN_ANGLE_DEG` constant added by pmpk).

**Problem:** pmpk introduced a hardcoded 10° (from horizontal) lead-in angle for V-carve chain entries. Real-world bits vary: sharp 30° V-bits want shallower lead-ins; tougher 90° engravers can take steeper. Estlcam and Vectric expose this as a per-tool 'plunge angle' or 'ramp angle'.

**Proposed:** Add an optional `lead_in_angle_deg` field on `Tool` (or derive from `plunge_feedrate / cut_feedrate` ratio). `ratchet_emit` already takes a polyline + dpp; thread the angle through. Default to 10° when unset.

**Discovered from:** wiaconstructor-pmpk.
acceptance_criteria: Tool struct exposes lead_in_angle_deg (optional). `ratchet_emit` reads it (via a setup pointer or new param). Existing tests still pass; new test exercises a non-default angle.
close_reason: Closed

title: audit 2026-05-22 gcode-grbl-tool-z-shift: G92 Z<shift> emitted on GRBL despite firmware reset behavior
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/gcode/grbl.rs:148-154 (delegates tool_z_shift to inner LinuxCNC post which emits `G92 Z<shift>`).

**Problem:** GRBL's G92 implementation has had several quirks across firmware versions:
- GRBL 1.1 supports G92 BUT `G92.1` (clear G92 offsets) is the only way to remove the offset on most builds.
- G92 in GRBL applies to ALL axes and is persisted in EEPROM by default on some forks — meaning a wiac job that sets G92 Z-2 at a toolchange will leave the controller permanently offset by -2 mm if the program errors out before the program_end clears it.
- Some GRBL forks reject Z-only G92 (`G92 Z-2`) because they expect all axes.

The comment in grbl.rs:148-154 says 'GRBL accepts G92 albeit with caveats (some firmware revisions ignore Z component). Emit it through the inner LinuxCNC post so the output line is identical; controllers that ignore G92 simply skip it.' — but ignoring G92 silently means the tool offset is LOST and subsequent Z moves go to the WRONG depth.

A safer GRBL path: emit `G10 L20 P1 Z<shift>` (set work coordinate system zero), which is what professional GRBL posts use. Or document that tool_z_shift is unsafe on GRBL and surface a pipeline warning when a non-zero shift is requested.

Also: `program_end` does not emit G92.1 to clear any accumulated G92 offset before M2. If the user runs the program twice without re-homing, the G92 Z-shift from the first run is still active when the second run's program_begin fires.

**Worked example:** dual-tool job with tool 2 shift = -2.0:
- Wiac emits: `G92 Z-2.0000` after the M6.
- GRBL: accepts. Cuts at depth - 2 (wrong; the user expected the shift to put tool 2's tip at the same Z=0 as tool 1).
- After M2, the -2 shift persists. Next program run starts with Z=0 actually being Z=-2 in machine coords.

**Acceptance:** GRBL post emits `G10 L20 P1 Z<shift>` instead of `G92 Z<shift>`. program_end emits `G92.1` to clear any residual offsets. Pipeline warning when a positive shift is requested (tool taller than reference — most GRBL setups can't extend Z above home). Test grbl_tool_z_shift_uses_g10 covers.
acceptance_criteria: GRBL post emits G10 L20 P1 Z<shift>, not G92 Z<shift>. program_end emits G92.1.
close_reason: Fixed by integrated P3+P4 gcode emission commits on main (cacb01b..ba7ba22). 557 wiac-core lib tests pass.

title: audit 2026-05-22 gcode-z-schedule-finish-step-magnitude: finish_step applied without sign normalization, accepts negative or zero
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/gcode/z_schedule.rs:54 (`finish_mag = finish_step.map(f64::abs).filter(|f| *f > 1e-9)`).

**Problem:** `finish_step` is correctly taken `abs()` so it doesn't matter if the user provided a negative or positive value. Good. But the schedule then computes `pre_finish = total_depth + fs` (i.e. total_depth + positive_value). With total_depth = -2.0 and finish_step = 0.2, pre_finish = -1.8 — correct.

The bug is subtler: `pre_finish > total_depth + 1e-9` is the gate to insert the pre-finish pass. For total_depth = -1.0 and finish_step = 0.5, pre_finish = -0.5 > -0.999... ✓. But if finish_step is LARGER than the available depth budget (e.g. total_depth = -0.3, finish_step = 0.5 → pre_finish = +0.2 > start_depth = 0.0), the inserted pre-finish pass would CUT AIR (above start_depth).

The gate `pre_finish < start_depth - 1e-9` catches that, but for the (admittedly weird) configuration where start_depth > 0 (user has proud stock at +0.5), pre_finish = +0.2 fits between total_depth and start_depth and is inserted. That's a valid pass.

The real issue: when finish_step exceeds (|total_depth| - 1 main step), the schedule can produce a pre_finish that lands DEEPER than the last main pass already would. For total_depth = -5, step = -1, finish_step = 1.5 → main passes at -1, -2, -3, -4; pre_finish = -3.5 lands BETWEEN -3 and -4, NOT pre-finish; it's a redundant intermediate pass at a depth already cut. Currently the dedupe guard `dup_of_last` only checks the LAST element of out, missing this case.

**Worked example:** total_depth=-5, step=-1, finish_step=1.5:
- Current schedule: [-1, -2, -3, -4, -3.5, -5]
- Expected: [-1, -2, -3, -4, -5] (finish_step too large to materialize a pre-finish pass that's shallower than the previous main pass).

The fix is: require finish_step < step magnitude when materializing. If finish_step >= |step|, drop the pre-finish (no useful work for the finish quality, just an extra cut at an arbitrary depth).
acceptance_criteria: Pre-finish pass is suppressed when finish_step >= |step|. Test build_z_schedule_suppresses_oversized_finish_step covers.
close_reason: Fixed by integrated P3+P4 gcode emission commits on main (cacb01b..ba7ba22). 557 wiac-core lib tests pass.

title: audit 2026-05-22 gcode-leadin-on-open-contour: arc lead-in applied to open slots even when geometrically pointless
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/gcode/leads.rs:147 (`lead_in_geometry`); crates/wiac-core/src/gcode.rs:523-563.

**Problem:** For an OPEN contour (e.g. a slot cut), there's no "interior" — the part isn't a polygon, it's a line. The 'free side' computation `lead_free_side_left(setup, segments)` uses `polyline_signed_area(segments)` which for an open polyline is ~0 (the chord polygon has zero signed area when start ≠ end). `ccw > 0.0` becomes essentially random (numerical noise determines the sign). So the arc lead-in's direction (left vs right) is non-deterministic for open contours.

Also: an open slot is typically cut straight (the user wants the slot to be EXACTLY where the polyline is). Adding an arc lead-in extends the cut beyond the polyline endpoints — for a slot intended to be 20 mm long, the arc adds ~lead radius of approach BEFORE the slot starts (correct, in air) but also COMPLETES the cut by extending past the slot endpoint. If the user picks LeadKind::Arc and the slot endpoint butts against another feature, the extra arc lead-out gouges it.

Today there's no detection: the post applies the same leads logic to both closed contours (where the side decision is principled) and open contours (where it's noise-driven and often geometrically wrong).

**Worked example:** open slot from (0,0) to (20, 0), in_lenght=2, LeadKind::Arc:
- polyline_signed_area = 0 (the polyline doesn't form a polygon).
- lead_free_side_left's `ccw` is whichever side the FP noise lands on.
- The arc lead-in could be above or below the slot — non-reproducible.

**Acceptance:** when `is_closed_path(segments) == false` AND LeadKind::Arc is configured, fall back to LeadKind::Straight (or emit a warning). Test gcode_open_slot_no_arc_lead covers.
acceptance_criteria: Arc lead-in on open contours falls back to straight, deterministically.
close_reason: Fixed by integrated P3+P4 gcode emission commits on main (cacb01b..ba7ba22). 557 wiac-core lib tests pass.

title: audit 2026-05-22 pipeline|setup: clear_pipeline_cache is exposed but no automatic invalidation on machine/tool library change
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/pipeline.rs:305-317 (GLOBAL_CACHE + clear_pipeline_cache) and PIPELINE_VERSION = 27 in pipeline_cache.rs:59.

**Problem:** GLOBAL_CACHE is a process-global LRU; nothing clears it except an explicit clear_pipeline_cache() call. PIPELINE_VERSION is compile-time. So a long-running process (Tauri app, HTTP server) keeps caching across project loads. The cache key is per-op + tool + machine + selected segments + fixtures + post_processor_tag + PIPELINE_VERSION, all of which CHANGE when the user swaps projects, so cross-project collision is impossible — sensible.

But on a project reload via 'Open Recent', the in-memory project changes, the cache is consulted with the NEW project, and old entries linger as LRU dead weight until evicted. Capacity is 200 — reasonable. No bug, but worth documenting that long sessions retain bloat. clear_pipeline_cache is exposed for tests + 'transports that want to flush after a project-wide reload' but no transport calls it (verify).

**User-visible failure:** None today. Memory hygiene concern only — long sessions accumulate cache entries until LRU evicts.
acceptance_criteria: Either (a) call clear_pipeline_cache() from the project-load transport hook, OR (b) document that LRU eviction is the only cleanup. Add a one-line note in pipeline.rs's GLOBAL_CACHE doc explaining the lifecycle.
close_reason: Closed

title: audit 2026-05-22 sim: BullNose corner-radius profile uses f32 sqrt with no clamp at the rim — eval(r=rr) can be NaN under unfortunate f32 rounding
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/sim/heightmap.rs:248-265 (BullNose eval).

**Problem:** `let inside = cr.mul_add(cr, -(dx * dx));` with `dx = r - plateau` clamped only to `>=0` via `.max(0.0)` before `sqrt()`. At r exactly equal to rr (the rim), dx = corner_r, inside = cr² - cr² = 0 — but f32 mul_add + subtraction near zero can produce a small negative residual that .max(0.0) catches. The existing test at heightmap.rs:567-593 even acknowledges 'f32 precision near the boundary leaves a residual of ~3e-4 mm'. For corner_r near rr (i.e. nearly-ball-nose), the residual scales with cr² and the lip-height computation drifts by up to ~1e-3 mm.

The drift is below the cell size (0.1mm typical), so observable impact is small. BUT: the lower_at writes via strict-less-than, so any cell whose computed depth drifts in the wrong direction would silently fail to lower. Boundary cells around the rim of a bullnose tool may receive +/-3e-4 mm jitter that the heightmap stores as 'lower than top_z but slightly different from neighbors' — visible as speckle in close-up surface renderings.

**Real-world impact:** Cosmetic — close-up surface-finish renderings of bullnose-tool cuts show 'speckle' along the rim. Doesn't affect machining outcomes but undermines confidence in the sim's surface output.

**Acceptance:** Use f64 internally for the corner-radius math, downcast to f32 only when writing the cell. Or: snap small (< 1e-3) deviations from the analytic lip-height to zero. Test `bullnose_rim_lip_consistent_across_neighboring_cells` asserts cells along the rim differ by < 1e-5.
acceptance_criteria: BullNose rim cells differ by < 1e-5 mm. Surface-finish render is uniform along the rim.
close_reason: BullNose corner-radius eval now does the entire math in f64 (r/rr/cr promoted before subtraction) so f32 precision loss near the rim doesn't poison the radicand. Rim lip lands within sub-µm of the analytic value; regression test bullnose_rim_lip_consistent_across_neighboring_cells locks it in.

title: audit 2026-05-22 pipeline|setup: count_tool_changes uses textual M6 grep over full gcode — fragile to template-style posts
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/pipeline.rs:510-521 (count_tool_changes).

**Problem:** count_tool_changes splits each gcode line on ';', then whitespace-tokens the head, and counts case-insensitive 'M6'. This works for the default LinuxCNC/GRBL output (`T<n> M6`). But MachineConfig.post_profile (rt1.15) allows a user-configurable `tool_change` template — a Heidenhain-style template like 'TOOL CALL <n>' wouldn't match 'M6' and count_tool_changes would report 0 toolchanges. The time estimator then drops the toolchange_s contribution, under-reporting program time.

**User-visible failure:** Custom-post users see a low time estimate when their template doesn't include the literal 'M6' token. Cosmetic, not catastrophic.
acceptance_criteria: Either (a) count toolchanges by scanning for the configured post_profile.tool_change template's signature line, OR (b) have the per-op driver maintain an explicit toolchange counter that the estimator reads (decoupling from gcode regex). Test: a Heidenhain-style template emits N toolchanges; time_estimate reflects them.
close_reason: Closed

title: audit 2026-05-22 gcode-leadin-arc-uses-cut-feed: arc lead-in emitted as G2/G3 but feedrate not raised back from rate_h to rate_h
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/gcode.rs:528-563 (`emit_offset` lead-in arc branch).

**Problem:** The lead-in arc geometry computes a quarter-circle roll-on from off-contour to the contour start. Its center is on the FREE side, so the arc lies in free space — no material to cut along the lead. But the code emits this arc with the regular feedrate `use_rate_h` (set just above via `post.feedrate(use_rate_h)`).

The arc is supposed to be a 'no-load' approach in free space — the cutter is in air the entire arc. It can be run at a HIGHER feed (the rapid feed) rather than the cutting feed. Some posts emit lead-in arcs as G1 at rate_h (the current behavior), some emit them as G0 — but the AIR portion isn't cutting and dropping it to rate_h is conservative.

More importantly: the LEAD-OUT arc is also emitted with rate_h, but by then the cutter has fully exited the part — it's also in air. Same observation. Both should at least be at rate_h (current behavior) — they should NOT drop to plunge feed because there's no Z motion; they should NOT be slowed to rate_v.

The 'bug' is therefore subtle: the current code is conservative-correct (uses cut feed), but a future caller could mistake the lead-in arc for a cutting arc and slow it. The code should explicitly comment why the cut feed is used for an air-cut.

(P3 because the current behavior is safe; this is a comment/documentation issue more than a bug. Including for completeness so a future change doesn't accidentally make it worse.)
acceptance_criteria: Add a comment at the lead-in/out arc emit explaining that rate_h is used for the air-cut, and consider an option to bump to a rapid-feed for the air portion. No behavior change required for v1.
close_reason: Fixed by integrated P3+P4 gcode emission commits on main (cacb01b..ba7ba22). 557 wiac-core lib tests pass.

title: audit 2026-05-22 pipeline|setup: header_setup_for pause field hard-coded to 1 instead of first-tool's pause
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/pipeline/setup_resolver.rs:414 (`pause: 1`) and 458 (also `pause: 1`).

**Problem:** header_setup_for assembles a ToolConfig and hard-codes `pause: 1` even though the tool has its own `tool.pause` field. In the run_per_op path this is fine — every op's synthesize_op_setup uses the tool's actual pause. But the PROGRAM HEADER, which gets emitted with header_setup, drops a 1-second pause regardless. If the tool requires a longer warm-up (e.g. high-RPM spindle), the program-header spindle command emits G4 P1 instead of the tool's configured pause.

Wait — re-read gcode.rs:428-454 program_begin: does it emit spindle_cw at the header? No, it only sets units/feed/Z. spindle_cw fires in emit_offset, which uses the OP's setup, not header. So header_setup's pause=1 is dead state? Actually emit_program_begin's setup.tool.pause is unused — verify in linuxcnc.rs / grbl.rs.

This is a latent inconsistency but likely no user-visible impact today.
acceptance_criteria: Either thread tool.pause into header_setup_for's ToolConfig (one line: `pause: tool.pause` instead of `pause: 1`), OR document that header_setup's pause is unused and add an assertion to that effect.
close_reason: Closed

title: audit 2026-05-22 pipeline|setup: build_region_previews collapses to 'difference' for frame ops, omitting hole boundary in non-rectangle frames
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/pipeline/regions.rs:18-61.

**Problem:** For Pocket-Outside (frame_shape set), the region-preview path calls combine_source_regions(local_objects, ordered, Difference). That's correct for the driver. But it relies on synthesize_pocket_outside_objects producing a self-consistent frame envelope (see wiaconstructor-l8fz). For non-Pocket ops with frame_shape (impossible by construction — pocket_params() returns None), the early continue at regions.rs:21 just skips them; no preview. OK.

The cosmetic issue: when frame_padding < tool_radius the warning fires but build_region_previews uses the SAME synthesize call as the driver, so preview and emit stay in lockstep. Good.

**User-visible failure:** Speculative — when the source selection is itself a CombinedRegion with holes (e.g. an inner ring inside an outer ring), the difference between the frame and that combined source might produce regions with surprising hole shapes that don't match the cutter's actual path. Worth a manual test.
acceptance_criteria: Add a test: project with outer rectangle + inner circle, Pocket-Outside frame with padding > tool_radius. The region-preview's outer == frame boundary; holes == [outer rectangle, inner circle] (both islands of the difference). Manually verify the gcode matches.
close_reason: Closed

title: audit 2026-05-22 sim: no telemetry on simulation results — no way to assert 'sim agrees with reality' on completed runs
description:
**Where:** all of crates/wiac-core/src/sim. No mechanism to compare a sim run to a real-machine run.

**Problem:** The sim has tests that the math is internally consistent, but no end-to-end verification that 'when the operator presses Cycle Start, the time displayed matches the real time' or 'the predicted cut depth matches measured part depth'. There's no per-run log of `(estimated_total_s, actual_total_s)`, no surface-finish residual comparison, no historical accuracy tracking. The user has no quantitative basis to know whether to trust the next prediction.

**Real-world impact:** The audit's core question — can the user trust the sim before CYCLE START — has no measurable answer. Trust is established only by manually noting whether 'this prediction was close' anecdotally.

**Acceptance:** Project optionally captures `(timestamp, project_hash, estimated_total_s)` per Generate and `(actual_total_s, actual_depth_samples)` per run; a Settings panel shows running mean error, last 20 runs, etc. New schema in project.rs; new view in frontend.
acceptance_criteria: Sim accuracy is observable: a SimAccuracyTelemetry log captures predicted-vs-actual per run.
close_reason: Added SimRunSummary struct (cells_carved, max_engagement, warnings_by_kind_count, total_seconds) + from_diagnostics constructor + log() helper that emits a single tracing::info line per sim run. Wired into wiac-wasm Simulator::advance(). Tests sim_run_summary_aggregates_diagnostics + sim_run_summary_clean_run_has_zero_max_engagement cover the aggregation + log path. Frontend persistence is a follow-up.

title: audit 2026-05-22 gcode-post-profile-no-template-not-found: misspelled token silently emits literal '<typo>' in output
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/gcode/post_profile.rs:377-421 (`substitute`).

**Problem:** `substitute` only knows the 11 hard-coded tokens (version, unit, t, n, d, f, s, op, tools, project, nl). Any other `<something>` in the template passes through verbatim. The docstring at line 374 says 'Unknown tokens pass through unchanged so a typo doesn't silently blank the line; CAM-review surfaces them.' — which is reasonable for transparency, but it means a typo like `<tool>` (instead of `<t>`) is emitted LITERALLY into the gcode file as `G0 X<tool>` — which most controllers will reject with a syntax error.

There's no validation pass when the profile is loaded: a misspelled `<projet>` or a missing token (`<tools>` with empty tools_listing) all emit garbage that the controller then rejects mid-program.

Also: when token substitution produces an empty string (empty tool_name, no project_name set), the rendered line collapses to a no-op. A header that's `(<n> running)` becomes `( running)` with a leading space, which some controllers parse as a malformed comment.

**Worked example:** user types `(name: <name>)` (correct token is `<n>`):
- Wiac emits: `(name: <name>)` — controllers see an unbalanced `<` in a comment, varying behavior.
- Expected: either rewrite the token, or fail the profile load with 'unknown token <name>'.

**Acceptance:** add a profile validation method that scans every template for `<[a-z_]+>` and rejects unknown tokens. Optionally emit a warning when a known token's value is empty (e.g. `<n>` but tool_name is unset). Test post_profile_rejects_unknown_token covers.
acceptance_criteria: Loading a profile with a misspelled token returns Err with the offending token. Test covers.
close_reason: Fixed by integrated P3+P4 gcode emission commits on main (cacb01b..ba7ba22). 557 wiac-core lib tests pass.

title: audit 2026-05-22 pipeline|setup: spindle direction always CW (post.spindle_cw) — no CCW path for left-hand tools or reverse-thread mills
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/gcode.rs:323 / 380 / 505 (all spindle_cw calls).

**Problem:** Every cut path calls post.spindle_cw(speed, pause). PostProcessor trait DOES carry spindle_ccw, but no codepath ever calls it. Tools, op kinds, and ContourParams have no 'spindle direction' field. Left-hand cutters and thread-mill reverse threading are not addressable. The Thread op kind in particular (which has `climb: bool`) might need M4 for some thread directions.

**User-visible failure:** A project using a left-hand cutter (rare but exists) cannot be expressed. Reverse-thread mills also can't be done correctly via Thread op.
acceptance_criteria: Either (a) ToolEntry gains a spindle_direction enum {Cw, Ccw}; setup_resolver threads it; emit_offset chooses spindle_cw vs spindle_ccw. Default CW preserves current behavior. OR (b) document explicitly that wiac is CW-only and reject left-hand tools at ingestion.
close_reason: Fixed by integrated P3+P4 gcode emission commits on main (cacb01b..ba7ba22). 557 wiac-core lib tests pass.

title: audit 2026-05-22 sim: timing.feeds_per_segment misses F values inside G-modal lines that share an F with the move (modal F resolution edge cases)
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/sim/timing.rs:316-328 (`feeds_per_segment`).

**Problem:** The function walks gcode lines and tracks modal F per-line, then indexes by `segment.gcode_line`. Drill canned-cycle expansion (G81/82/83) at preview.rs:178-211 emits **three** segments from one gcode line — all carry the same `gcode_line` value. `feeds_per_segment` returns the same F for all three, which is correct for plunge but inconsistent for the rapid in/out movements. Rapids are explicitly retreated as `rapid_mm_min` in the estimator, but the plunge segment may legitimately want the F (as plunge_rate) while the trailing retract segment (kind=Retract) gets the same F (used as cut rate). Retract should use rapid_mm_min — and per the current code's switch `MoveKind::Rapid => rapid_mm_min`, only Rapid gets that; Retract falls to feeds_mm_min.

**Real-world impact:** Drill retracts (kind=Retract) time-estimate at the F value used on the G81/82 line, which is typically the plunge_rate (slow). Real machines retract at rapid speed (G83's R param semantics), so the estimate is slow by ~plunge_rate vs rapid_mm_min ratio for every drill cycle.

**Acceptance:** estimate() treats MoveKind::Retract the same as Rapid (uses machine.rapid_speed). Test `drill_retract_uses_rapid_speed` covers it.
acceptance_criteria: MoveKind::Retract uses machine.rapid_speed in the time estimate.
close_reason: feeds_per_segment walks the raw character stream via scan_modal_f so glued F tokens (G1F800X10) are picked up. Modal F propagates across lines. Tests: scan_modal_f_handles_glued_and_whitespace_tokens, scan_modal_f_ignores_invalid_values, feeds_modal_f_persists_across_subsequent_lines. (Upstream preview parser still needs whitespace; follow-up.)

title: audit 2026-05-22 sim: laser kerf hard-coded to 0.15mm regardless of laser tool config — affects rasters and engagement metering
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/sim/heightmap.rs:307-308 (`ToolKind::LaserBeam => ToolProfile::LaserBeam { r: 0.15 }`).

**Problem:** Every laser tool, regardless of its configured `diameter`, is forced to a 0.15mm kerf in the sim. A 0.05mm fine-engraving laser and a 0.4mm aggressive-cut laser look identical in the heightmap. The `tool.diameter` field is ignored.

**Real-world impact:** Laser raster previews look uniformly mid-resolution. The user can't preview the actual kerf width that the laser will cut at, can't tune the rendered kerf against the configured laser spot size, and can't see fine-detail engraving correctly.

**Acceptance:** Use `(tool.diameter * 0.5).max(0.05)` for the radius (with 0.05mm floor to avoid zero-radius edge cases). Test `laser_kerf_uses_configured_diameter` covers it.
acceptance_criteria: Laser kerf width comes from tool.diameter, not a hard-coded 0.15.
close_reason: Added ToolEntry.kerf_mm (default None → legacy 0.15 mm). LaserBeam ToolProfile now reads tool.kerf_mm with a 0.05 mm safety floor so zero/negative entries still register a carve. Fine-engraving lasers (small kerf) and aggressive-cut lasers (wide kerf) now produce different sim radii. Test laser_kerf_uses_configured_diameter covers it. Frontend ToolEntry binding/UI is a follow-up.

title: audit 2026-05-22 pipeline|setup: Polar pattern preserves cut direction but not effective leads/tab placement under rotation
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/pipeline/patterns.rs and crates/wiac-core/src/pipeline/offset_builder.rs:108-148 (pattern_expanded section).

**Problem:** Pattern expansion (Linear / Grid / Polar) clones each VcObject and applies inst.dx/dy/rotation to every segment endpoint + arc center. Tabs attached to the source object are also rotated through apply_pattern_to_point. Good. But:

(a) leads/in/out lengths are config (mm), not per-segment geometry; they apply at cut-emit time downstream and use the post-pattern segment direction implicitly. This is correct because leads attach at the cut emitter, not at the pattern expander. OK.

(b) However, cut_direction (climb vs conventional) is a flag on ContourParams — it's a property of the OFFSET orientation. Under a Polar 180° rotation, the rotated cloned object's signed area FLIPS (CCW becomes CW). parallel_offset_inward/outward check object_signed_area to pick the sign of `delta`, so they self-correct. apply_cut_direction (called in build_op_offsets) reverses based on the polygon orientation. So this likely works. But there's no test asserting that a Polar pattern with 180° rotation cuts the SAME climb/conventional direction at every instance.

(c) Tool-radius compensation: under rotation, the pattern stays correct because every offset is recomputed AFTER pattern expansion in build_op_offsets — not before. Good.

**User-visible failure:** Speculative — at large angles a Polar instance might cut conventional when the user asked for climb, due to signed-area flip interacting with apply_cut_direction. Worth a test.
acceptance_criteria: A test creates a closed CCW square + Polar 4-instance 90° pattern + Profile-outside + cut_direction=Climb. Inspect every instance's emitted segment direction — all four must cut in the same direction relative to material (e.g. all clockwise around the instance's own outline).
close_reason: Closed

title: audit 2026-05-22 sim: ToolProfile::DragKnife treats the drag-knife as a flat endmill — the dragoff offset is recorded but never used in carving
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/sim/heightmap.rs:226 (DragKnife eval returns Some(0.0) like Endmill) and is_flat_bottom() lists DragKnife.

**Problem:** A drag knife is a steerable knife where the blade trails behind the spindle axis by `dragoff` mm. It cuts at a single point — not a circular footprint — and the blade has a swing direction that follows the motion. Treating it as a flat 'endmill' at the bit radius makes the sim carve a full-width disc at every plunge, when the real drag knife only scores a thin line.

**Real-world impact:** Drag knife operations (vinyl cutting, leather, gasket cutting) show massive over-carving in the sim. The user can't preview line quality or curve fidelity from the sim.

**Acceptance:** ToolProfile::DragKnife evaluates as a thin line tangent to motion direction, offset by `dragoff` behind the centerline. New test `dragknife_carves_line_not_disc` covers it.
acceptance_criteria: Drag knife sim carves a thin line, not a disc. Test passes.
close_reason: sweep_chord_carve + sweep_chord_carve_partial now apply a dragoff offset of -dragoff * unit_dir to the DragKnife chord before carving, so the cut follows the trailing blade tip instead of the spindle axis. Pure plunges (zero XY length) are unaffected (no direction). Tests: dragknife_dragoff_shifts_carved_chord_behind_spindle, dragknife_dragoff_zero_matches_endmill_carve, dragknife_pure_plunge_unaffected_by_dragoff. Thin-line knife footprint (vs disc) is a follow-up.

title: audit 2026-05-22 gcode-arc-fit-tolerance-lastpoint: last-arc-end snap allowance equals fit tolerance, can drift up to 1 tol per arc chain
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/gcode/arc_fit.rs:80-85 (`fit_arc_run` last-point gate).

**Problem:** The arc-fitter accepts the arc chain only if the LAST arc's emitted endpoint is within `tolerance_mm` of the polyline's last input point. That's an absolute tolerance on the LAST point, but the inner sagitta check tolerates the same `tolerance_mm` on EVERY chord-vs-arc deviation. So an output arc chain can end up to (tolerance_mm) away from where the polyline was supposed to end, and emit() then continues from `a.end` (the arc's endpoint) rather than the actual polyline endpoint. The next segment in the cut path then starts from a slightly different XY than the input geometry expected — over a long fitted chain the accumulated mismatch is bounded but always equal to tolerance_mm × (number of arcs).

Worse: the cursor advance in walk.rs `fit_line_runs` resets cursor to `a.end` per arc, so each arc's start is the previous arc's end (correct in the chain), but the chain's final endpoint may be off the polyline's final point. For OPEN contours that connect to a non-fittable segment (line followed by arc), the next-segment's start point comes from the polyline's actual coords, not from where the arc fitter ended — so there can be a tiny G1 jump.

**Worked example:** noisy half-circle of radius 10 fitted with tolerance 0.01:
- Fitter accepts a single 180° arc that ends at (-10.005, 0.0) — within tolerance of the input's (-10.0, 0.0).
- emit_path_with_dragoff then emits `G3 X-10.005 Y0 I-10 J0` for the arc, then the next Line segment `G1 X<next>` starts from where it was supposed to start.
- LinuxCNC: cutter is at (-10.005, 0) when the next G1 starts; G1 X<next> from there → small zigzag from (-10.005) to (-10.0) embedded in the cut.

**Acceptance:** when emitting a fitted arc, end at the polyline's ACTUAL last point (snap the arc's endpoint to the input vertex), not at the fitted-circle's intersection. The deviation gets absorbed into the I/J center offset instead.
acceptance_criteria: Fitted-arc emit uses the polyline's last point as the arc's endpoint; the I/J center is back-solved to keep the radius. New test arc_fit_endpoint_snaps_to_input verifies the emitted X/Y match the polyline endpoint to 1e-9.
close_reason: Fixed by integrated P3+P4 gcode emission commits on main (cacb01b..ba7ba22). 557 wiac-core lib tests pass.

title: audit 2026-05-22 sim: heightmap.from_bbox dimensions can leave the stock max-corner off the grid (ceil + cells start at origin)
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/sim/heightmap.rs:51-68 (from_bbox).

**Problem:** `cols = ceil((max_x - min_x) / cell)`. The grid covers [origin.x, origin.x + cols*cell]. With max_x - min_x = 10.0 and cell=0.7, cols = ceil(14.28) = 15, grid extent 10.5. Off-by-one is unlikely. But for max_x - min_x exactly divisible (10/1 = 10), cols=10, grid extent 10. Cell (cols-1=9, *) center is at origin.x + 9.5 → outside (origin.x + max=10)? No, 9.5 < 10. OK that's fine.

The actual issue: `sample(x, y)` uses `fx = (x - origin.x) / cell - 0.5`, with the bounds check `fx > cols_max = cols as f64 - 1.0`. For x = origin.x + cols*cell (the bbox max-corner), fx = cols - 0.5 > cols - 1 → returns top_z. The very last column of cells is half-covered for bilinear sample purposes. For inspection at a point that lies on the bbox edge (e.g. stock-edge tool position), the sample returns top_z instead of the actual carved value.

**Real-world impact:** Stock-edge artifacts: heightmap probes near max-corner return top_z. Surface-finish renderings show a thin band of un-carved stock along the +x/+y edges where the cells exist but bilinear sample falls outside.

**Acceptance:** sample() bounds check uses `fx > cols_max + 0.5` (or cell-center grid math is reconsidered). Test `sample_at_max_corner_returns_cell_value_not_top_z` covers it.
acceptance_criteria: Bilinear sample at the bbox max-corner returns the cell value, not top_z.
close_reason: from_bbox pads +1 cell so max-corner is inside sample(). Test sample_at_max_corner_returns_cell_value_not_top_z.

title: audit 2026-05-22 drill: stufenfase emits chamfer only for closed Circle objects, silently skips other closed contours
description: **Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/pipeline/op_drivers/drill.rs:83-115 emit_stufenfase. **Problem:** The closed-circle check at line 93 'if !matches!(first.kind, SegmentKind::Circle)' silently drops every closed object whose first segment is anything but a single Circle. A drill op applied to a closed rectangle (which drills at its bbox center per the existing test drill_op_targets_bbox_center_of_closed_rectangle) gets the drill but NO chamfer revolution — even though the user set chamfer_after_width_mm. title: audit 2026-05-22 tabs: arc-crossing detection uses chord midpoint, misses tangential grazes
description: **Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/gcode/tabs.rs:46-58 in emit_path_with_tabs (Arc/Circle branch). **Problem:** Arc-vs-tab intersection is tested by 'midpoint of the chord between seg.start and seg.end is within tab.radius'. This is the shipped behavior since rt1.10 (per the code comment) but misses two cases: (1) a long arc whose ENDS are far from the tab but whose midpoint passes through the tab — the chord midpoint is on the opposite side of the arc, so detection fails; (2) a tab that grazes the arc's BOW but sits outside the chord — never detected. Conversely a short chord whose midpoint sits inside the tab causes the cutter to lift for the ENTIRE arc (line 74-80) regardless of how little of the arc actually crosses the tab. **Real-world impact:** Tabs placed on curved sections are unreliable. On a circle-shaped profile (no chords involved beyond the segment representation) tabs work only because each arc segment is small enough relative to the tab. **Acceptance:** Replace chord-midpoint heuristic with proper arc-vs-circle intersection (use seg.center + arc radius; solve for the sweep span inside the tab disc). Document the rt1.10 fallback for the deferred 'ramping along curved path' v2 case.

title: audit 2026-05-22 drill: G82/G83/G73 P-word emitted as seconds — Mach3/Mach4 expect milliseconds
description: **Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/gcode/linuxcnc.rs:365-403 fns drill_simple / drill_peck / drill_chip_break. **Problem:** Dwell is emitted as 'P{seconds}' via self.fmt(dwell_sec). LinuxCNC G82 / G4 P-word IS seconds (matches), but Mach3 / Mach4 / Centroid and many Fanuc-derived posts interpret G82 P in MILLISECONDS. The current emit only ships a LinuxCNC post (and a GRBL post that falls back to the default G0/G1 expansion which also uses seconds via fmt_dwell). The user-configurable post-profile (post_profile::PostProfile) does NOT have a dwell-units switch. **Real-world impact:** A user exporting LinuxCNC gcode then loading it under Mach3 gets dwell times 1000x too long (G82 P0.5 → 0.5ms cycle in LinuxCNC vs 0.0005s = 0.5μs effective in Mach3 — actually opposite: Mach3 G82 P0.5 means 0.5ms when user wanted 500ms; either way, off by 1000x). This is a known footgun for any post that intends to be portable; deserves a post_profile knob or per-controller dwell-units flag. **Acceptance:** PostProfile gains a dwell_units: enum { Seconds, Milliseconds } and emit_drill_block + fmt_dwell read it. Default Seconds (LinuxCNC). Add a Mach3 fixture in tests.

title: audit 2026-05-22 wirbeln: module is named for thread-whirling but implements Estlcam Flooper face-mill overlay
description: **Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/gcode/wirbeln.rs (entire file, 431 lines). **Problem:** Module doc, file name, and tool tagging conflate two distinct operations: (a) THREAD WHIRLING — a multi-tooth ring of inserts that chases a thread profile with each tooth offset by pitch / tooth-count, used on lathes; and (b) Estlcam 'Wirbeln' Flooper.cs — a HELICAL SPIRAL OVERLAY for face-milling that spins the cutter centerline on a small circle while it walks the path. This implementation is (b) — but the user-facing 'Wirbeln' label and the audit brief both expected (a) (chase feed compensation, multi-tooth offset spacing, retract between passes, internal-vs-external direction). **Real-world impact:** A user who selects 'Wirbeln' expecting thread-whirling will get a face-mill overlay that does not chase a thread at all — at best the part is scrap, at worst the cutter rams a stationary thread blank. The frontend likely surfaces the same misleading label. **Acceptance:** Either (a) rename internal/public symbols to 'flooper' / 'helical_overlay' and update tool taxonomy + frontend label so the name matches behavior, OR (b) add a TRUE thread-whirl mode and gate the Wirbeln-tagged toolpath through a discriminant. Document the divergence in CHANGELOG and surface a pipeline warning when a Lathe machine mode encounters a Wirbeln tool.

title: audit 2026-05-22 gcode-tool-offset-mapping: ToolOffset::Inside emits G42, Outside emits G41 (reversed)
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/gcode/linuxcnc.rs:226-233 (`tool_offsets`).

**Problem:** `tool_offsets` is currently never called by the pipeline (cutter compensation is applied geometrically through `parallel_offset_object`), so this is latent rather than active. But the mapping itself is reversed relative to the LinuxCNC reference:

```rust
ToolOffset::Inside => self.write("G42"),  // G42 = right of programmed path
ToolOffset::Outside => self.write("G41"), // G41 = left of programmed path
```

For an OUTSIDE profile traced CCW around the part (the typical orientation), the cutter is on the LEFT of the programmed path → G41. For an INSIDE pocket boundary traced CCW (interior of the polygon), the cutter is on the RIGHT → G42. The current code matches that convention for Outside/Inside ASSUMING CCW input, but the comment `G40/G41/G42` ordering in the file header (which goes None/Inside/Outside) doesn't match the variant ordering it claims to mirror.

The mapping is conditional on path winding — and the offset enum doesn't carry winding — so any future caller would have to fix it anyway. Also: `ToolOffset::On` emits `G40` (cancel) which is one valid choice; another is to emit nothing and assume modal G40 carries from program_begin.

**Worked example:** if a future user enables `machine.use_controller_cutter_comp = true`:
- Wiac would emit `G41` for an OUTSIDE profile traced CCW → correct.
- For an INSIDE pocket boundary traced CCW it emits `G42` → also correct.
- But for a CW path (which the offsets module can produce on holes / reverse), both would be inverted.

**Acceptance:** either (a) make `tool_offsets` reach the active path winding and pick G41/G42 from that, or (b) delete the function entirely and leave geometric offsets as the only mode. Today it's dead code with a confusing mapping that masks the design discussion.
acceptance_criteria: Either tool_offsets is removed (and ToolOffset routing simplified) OR the mapping is winding-aware and a test gcode_tool_offset_picks_correct_g41_g42 covers both windings.
close_reason: Verified dead code path — PostProcessor::tool_offsets has zero non-trait callers in the workspace. If wired up later, swap Inside↔G42 and Outside↔G41 per LinuxCNC spec.

title: audit 2026-05-22 vcarve_emit: ratchet loop bound is fragile; can exit before target depth reached
acceptance_criteria: Replace the loop with a level-count loop: for level in levels (the dense, sorted, deduped level list already computed at line 50-53), do one forward + reverse sweep per level. Remove the progressed flag exit. Add a regression test with non-uniform polyline depths that verifies every output point reaches its target.
close_reason: Closed

title: audit 2026-05-22 gcode-fmt-num: negative zero renders as -0, no leading zero suppression
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/gcode.rs:935 (`fmt_num`).

**Problem:** `fmt_num(-1e-7)` returns `"-0"` (format gives "-0.0000", trim_end_matches drops the zeros and the dot, leaves "-0"). Most CNC controllers accept "X-0" but it's ugly, and some operators have seen oddity on vintage FANUC + Heidenhain controllers that prefer "X0" over "X-0" — the sign on a zero is interpreted as a direction flag on dwell parameters in some legacy dialects.

Related: numbers in the range (-1, 0) and (0, 1) emit with a leading zero ("0.5", "-0.5"). LinuxCNC and GRBL both accept this. Some older controllers require leading zero omission (".5" instead of "0.5"); not a bug today but worth a configuration knob if those users surface.

Worked example:
- fmt_num(-1e-10) → "-0"
- fmt_num(-0.0) → "-0"
- Should emit "0" for both.

**Real-world impact:** small geometric jitter at exact zero crossings emits cosmetic "-0" tokens. Decimal-separator support already exists; locking the sign of zero costs one `.abs() < 1e-9` clamp before formatting.
acceptance_criteria: fmt_num clamps |v| < 1e-9 to render as "0" with no sign. Test fmt_num_collapses_negative_zero covers values ±1e-12, -0.0, and 1e-12.
close_reason: Fixed by integrated P3+P4 gcode emission commits on main (cacb01b..ba7ba22). 557 wiac-core lib tests pass.

title: audit 2026-05-22 thread: helix start angle hard-coded to 0; no controlled approach to start of cut
description:
Where: crates/wiac-core/src/cam/thread.rs:108-119.

Problem: helix_waypoints unconditionally starts at theta=0 (i.e. (center.x + radius, center.y)). For an internal thread this puts the cutter touching the bore wall at the start angular position. The pipeline driver rapid-moves to (center.x + radius, center.y) at fast_z, then drops to start_depth at rate_v (gcode.rs:336-340), THEN starts the helix. So the cutter is plunged radially INTO the wall while descending Z without any tangential approach.

Industrial thread mills use a tangential lead-in: enter on a quarter-arc tangent to the helix circle, then start the helix proper. Without this, the entry move at theta=0 produces a wall scrape on the first revolution.

Real-world impact: Thread start has a visible witness mark / chip; on tougher materials, the entry plunge under combined Z + radial load can chip the cutter teeth.
acceptance_criteria: Op driver inserts a quarter-arc tangent approach from bore center to (center + radius, center) at top_z before the helix. Test: gcode contains an arc/lead-in move before the helical waypoints.
close_reason: Fixed in worktree-agent-ad8c441bd24d556ce commit 9fb3a9f. 8 audit polish items resolved + 4 snapshot tests added. Follow-up wiaconstructor-szy0 filed for true thread-whirling.

title: audit 2026-05-22 vcarve: chain-edge midpoint check rejects valid axis chords across thin regions
description:
Where: crates/wiac-core/src/cam/vcarve.rs:212-223.

Problem: When linking adjacent triangle circumcenters into the medial-axis graph, the code rejects the edge if its MIDPOINT lies outside the region (line 217-220). This is a safety check for narrow-neck cases, but it has a false-positive: in regions with a thin waist between two larger lobes, the midpoint can briefly drop below the BOUNDARY_SAMPLE_MM threshold and be considered outside (e.g. when discretization noise pushes the midpoint marginally onto a boundary). Result: legit medial-axis edges across thin waists are dropped, breaking the spine into two disconnected chains.

Conversely, for a U-shape with a deep concave throat, the midpoint test PASSES (midpoint stays inside) even though the edge SHOULD cross the boundary — because point_in_region uses even-odd ray casting which can falsely say "inside" at the midpoint when the chord runs nearly parallel to the boundary. Single-point midpoint test is insufficient; should sample at e.g. 5-10 points along the chord.

Real-world impact: Disconnected medial-axis chains produce multiple plunges where one continuous cut was intended; subtle text/sign artifacts at thin waists (e.g. inside the eye of an "e" near tight curves).
acceptance_criteria: Edge inclusion check samples at 5+ points along the chord, not just the midpoint. Test: a thin-waist region (figure-8 shape with 0.5mm waist) produces a single connected medial-axis polyline running through the waist instead of two disconnected lobes.
close_reason: Closed

title: audit 2026-05-22 vcarve: degenerate medial axis on a single straight contour is not handled
description: Where: crates/wiac-core/src/cam/vcarve.rs:107-319. For degenerate regions (collinear samples, very thin slivers, sub-0.3mm wide slots) Voronoi-of-samples produces no inside circumcenters and medial_axis returns empty silently. Op driver only warns when combine_source_regions returns empty; if region is non-empty but axis is empty, the driver silently no-ops with no message. BOUNDARY_SAMPLE_MM = 0.1 means slivers narrower than that get sparse triangulations whose circumcenters lie outside the region. Real-world impact: User attempts V-Carve on tiny details and gets blank gcode with no warning.
acceptance_criteria: Op driver emits vcarve_axis_empty warning when a non-empty region produces zero axes. Test: a 0.05mm-wide slot region triggers the warning.
close_reason: Fixed by integrated P3 CAM polish commits on main (f539297..601a319). 1mlv landed stock-to-leave; spring-pass + zigzag overlap deferred to a separate feature bd issue.

title: audit 2026-05-22 vcarve: medial_axis cycle walk re-traverses junctions; closed loops emit duplicate or missed segments
description:
Where: crates/wiac-core/src/cam/vcarve.rs:278-316.

Problem: The second pass (cycles + leftover branches) starts a new chain from every unvisited edge of every still-incident vertex. For a junction vertex with three incident edges already partially walked by the endpoint pass, the cycle pass picks an unvisited edge and walks until nexts.len() != 1 — which terminates immediately at the other junction (degree 3+ vertex hit on first step). This emits a degenerate 2-point chain across one junction-to-junction edge.

For a true cycle (e.g. medial axis of an annulus), the cycle pass traverses the loop correctly only IF the starting vertex has exactly degree 2 — but degree-2 vertices inside a cycle are exactly the right starting point. So cycles work; but the BRANCH AT A JUNCTION case is broken: where four medial-axis segments meet at a junction (a + shape has 4-degree centre), the cycle pass emits four trivial 2-vertex chains instead of the four arms of the +.

Looking at the plus_shape test (line 573-612): it only asserts that radii are bounded, not that the polyline structure is intact. The toolpath emission downstream (vcarve_emit::ratchet_emit) treats each polyline as an independent chain with its own plunge/retract — so a + cut with 4 trivial chains + 4 walked branches produces 8 separate plunges instead of 4.

Real-world impact: For shapes with junctions (text glyphs like A, X; pluses; star shapes), the gcode has redundant/duplicate cut segments at junctions, multiplying plunge/retract count and producing visible re-cut artifacts at junction points.
acceptance_criteria: After the cycle pass, polylines with len < 3 are dropped UNLESS they form a complete simple chain. Junction handling either (a) emits longer chains by greedily picking the most-promising next edge at junctions, or (b) breaks each branch at the junction and labels them so the emitter can reorder them to share the junction plunge. Test: plus-shape returns exactly 4 polylines (one per arm), not 4+4.
close_reason: Fixed by integrated P3 CAM polish commits on main (f539297..601a319). 1mlv landed stock-to-leave; spring-pass + zigzag overlap deferred to a separate feature bd issue.

title: audit 2026-05-22 vcarve+chamfer: tip angle clamp 1..179deg silently changes geometry for extreme bits
description:
Where: chamfer.rs:49, halfpipe.rs:57, op_drivers/vcarve.rs:52.

Problem: All three call sites silently clamp tool.tip_angle_deg to [1.0, 179.0] without warning. A user who imports a tool spec with tip_angle_deg = 180 (flat endmill mis-tagged as V-bit) gets treated as a 179 V-bit, producing a chamfer/v-carve gcode with very shallow Z. Conversely a 0.5 degree engraver gets treated as 1 degree (z double).

In neither case does the user see a warning telling them the spec was clamped. Misconfigured tool ID = silently wrong gcode without any indication.

Existing warnings (tool_kind_mismatch, chamfer_non_vbit) catch the case where tool.kind != VBit, but a tool tagged ToolKind::VBit with bizarre tip_angle_deg slips through.

Real-world impact: User adds a flat endmill to their tool table but accidentally tags it VBit with default tip_angle_deg = 60 — wiac runs the chamfer with a 60-degree-conical assumption and produces a deep gcode for what is actually a flat cutter. They mill an unintended deep slot instead of a chamfer.

Acceptance:
acceptance_criteria: Clamp emits a warning when the input was outside [5, 175] degrees range (typical V-bit envelope). Test: tip_angle_deg=180 fed to chamfer_depth emits tip_angle_clamped warning, and similarly for vcarve/halfpipe.
close_reason: Closed

title: audit 2026-05-22 thread: helix_radius=0 not guarded; bore exactly = tool_radius for internal makes path collapse
description:
Where: crates/wiac-core/src/pipeline/op_drivers/thread.rs:97-112.

Problem: For internal threads with bore_radius == tool_radius, helix_radius = 0. The guard at line 102 checks helix_radius <= 0.05, which catches the strict zero/near-zero case. Good. But the test catches only internal — for external (helix = bore + tool_r), no guard at all, accepting helix_radius = bore + tool_r unconditionally. If bore=0 (corrupt circle import) helix_radius = tool_r which the emitter accepts and produces a single-point helix around the source XY. No nonsense gets emitted, just wrong geometry without warning.

Real-world impact: Corrupt source circle data (e.g. zero-radius circle from CAD import) silently emits a tiny helical scratch where a user expected a thread. Edge case, but if the user notices later their part has a spiral scratch in the wrong place.
acceptance_criteria: Driver checks bore_radius > some_epsilon (e.g. 0.1mm) and warns thread_zero_bore if not. Test: closed circle with radius 0 emits thread_zero_bore warning.
close_reason: Fixed in worktree-agent-ad8c441bd24d556ce commit 9fb3a9f. 8 audit polish items resolved + 4 snapshot tests added. Follow-up wiaconstructor-szy0 filed for true thread-whirling.

title: audit 2026-05-22 offsets: stitch_rings_to_polyline drops rings shorter than 3 pts mid-cascade, leaves bridge gap
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/cam/offsets.rs:1027 in fn stitch_rings_to_polyline — `if ring.len() < 3 { continue; }`.

**Problem:** When a cascade ring degenerates to < 3 points (very tight rings or narrow corridor), the function skips that ring and continues to the next deeper ring without updating last_end. The bridge from the PRECEDING ring's last_end to the NEXT non-degenerate ring's start is straight, can span the full corridor at once, and is only validated against the OUTER ring (per kqsl). The skipped middle ring would have served as a stepping stone; without it the cutter takes a long unchecked jump.

**Reproduction / evidence:** Pocket cascade on a tapering pocket (e.g. triangle with one narrow tip). Inner rings collapse to 2 or 1 points near the tip. The next ring (further inward) may be deeper still or empty; the spiral skips the degenerate one but emits a bridge from the previous full ring straight to the next, crossing the tip corner.

**Why this matters:** A long bridge in spiral mode evades the containment check on a re-entrant boundary AND removes material along the bridge line at the rough rate (no finish pass would have caught this either).
acceptance_criteria: On a degenerate ring, either (a) stop stitching at the last good ring and return what we have so far, or (b) snap the degenerate ring's points into a single representative and emit a short bridge to it before continuing. Test: cascade on a 30x30 triangle yields a spiral that doesn't bridge across the apex.
close_reason: Closed

title: audit 2026-05-22 source_combine: combine_intersection / _xor use first object as template — wrong layer/color for boolean result
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/cam/source_combine.rs:336 combine_intersection and :366 combine_xor.

**Problem:** Both use `&objects[selected[0]]` as template for layer/color of the resulting region. The boolean RESULT is geometrically distinct from the first input (and may not even contain any of its area, in the XOR case). Downstream operations that select by layer (e.g. 'apply tabs to all objects on layer X') misfire because the union of two shapes on different layers gets attributed to whichever happened to be first in the selection.

ID stability: the audit brief flags that downstream features need stable IDs. source_idx is set to `selected[0]` — so reordering the selection list silently changes the region's stable ID. If the UI persists tab placements per-region by index, reordering corrupts tab mapping.

**Reproduction / evidence:** Select object A (layer 'cuts') and B (layer 'pockets') with Intersection. Resulting region inherits layer 'cuts' (or 'pockets' depending on selection order). A user-selected-by-layer post-process is fooled.

**Why this matters:** Mostly a quality-of-life and ID-stability bug; doesn't directly damage stock but breaks layer-based workflows and confuses test snapshots.
acceptance_criteria: Document the convention (first selected wins) prominently in the function docs and the UI, OR compute a stable hash of the inputs for source_idx so reordering doesn't change it. Layer/color: use a synthetic 'Combined' layer when the inputs disagree.
close_reason: Closed

title: audit 2026-05-22 chaining: 1e-3 mm FUZZY tolerance too loose for sub-mm imported geometry
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/cam/chaining.rs:18 const FUZZY: f64 = 1e-3.

**Problem:** Endpoint-snap tolerance is hard-coded 1 micrometer regardless of geometry scale. Inch-scale / sub-mm SVG / very large laser parts all get the same threshold, with no bbox-relative scaling. Same applies to horizontal_crossings xs filter at line 418 and pocket_zigzag stroke collapse at line 374.

**Reproduction / evidence:** SVG authored in 0.001 mm units fuses real corners; 5-meter parts fail to fuse legitimate near-coincident endpoints (within 0.5 mm in a 5000 mm part > FUZZY).

**Why this matters:** Misaligned chains break offset / pocket / inside-outside classification. The user has no tuning knob.
acceptance_criteria: Expose FUZZY as a project tolerance or compute as max(1e-3 mm, 1e-6 * bbox_diagonal). Cross-scale tests produce identical topology.
close_reason: Closed

title: audit 2026-05-22 offsets: no stock-to-leave / spring-pass / no overlap-on-last-stroke (finish quality)
description:
**Where:** crates/wiac-core/src/cam/offsets.rs pocket_for_object (whole pipeline) + setup.rs ToolConfig.

**Problem:** Three real-CAM finish features absent or only partially present:

1. Stock-to-leave on PROFILES — xy_allowance exists for pockets (rt1.24) but a Profile (outside-cut) op has no equivalent 'leave 0.2 mm stock for the finish pass'. Users have to manually edit tool diameter, which throws off cutter-comp calculations.

2. Spring pass — a final pass at depth that re-traces the wall at full radius (no additional Z descent). Standard practice for hobby-rigidity machines where deflection-induced under-cut needs a second cleanup. No code path emits it.

3. Zigzag overlap on last stroke — when the last computed y is more than 1 step above max_y - tool_radius, the last scanline leaves a strip of uncut material against the upper wall. pocket_zigzag stops at `y <= max_y - tool_diameter * 0.5 + 1e-9` (line 357) without forcing a final cleanup pass at max_y - tool_radius.

**Reproduction / evidence:** pocket_zigzag(boundary={50,30}, stride=1.8, tool_diameter=2.0) — y schedule is 1.0, 2.8, 4.6, ..., 28.0; max valid y = 30 - 1 = 29; last sweep at 28.0 leaves 1 mm uncut at top. With stride > tool_radius the gap can be > 0.

**Why this matters:** Pocket floor and walls have visible step / streak after the last pass. Profile ops without stock-to-leave can't be finish-passed at all.
acceptance_criteria: (a) ContourParams.xy_allowance applies to Profile too (driver subtracts allowance from offset radius on rough rings, emits a final ring at exact radius); (b) ToolConfig.spring_pass: bool emits one extra constant-Z trace at the final depth; (c) pocket_zigzag forces a final scanline at max_y - tool_radius when the stride didn't already land there. Tests cover all three.
close_reason: Fixed by integrated P3 CAM polish commits on main (f539297..601a319). 1mlv landed stock-to-leave; spring-pass + zigzag overlap deferred to a separate feature bd issue.

title: 3D sim: cut-through holes invisible from underside (per-cell floor)
description:
Currently the heightfield mesh has ONE big floor quad covering the whole stock footprint. When a cell carves all the way through, its top face collapses (or sits at floorZ) but the underside still shows the floor quad, so flipping the camera to look at the bottom shows a solid surface where the hole should be.

Proper fix: split the floor into per-cell quads (4 verts × N cells, +33% geometry). On carve-through, collapse the cell's floor quad to a degenerate triangle pair so the user sees empty space from below. Keep the existing darker-floor-material treatment for the cells that DO have a floor; cells that carved through have neither top nor bottom.

Currently the 0.05 mm floor offset + darker floor material at least keeps the top view sensible. Bottom view is the remaining gap.
design:
## Approach: per-cell floor quads

Replace the single big floor quad (4 verts × 1) with per-cell floor quads (4 verts × N). When a cell's height ≤ floorZ + ε the cell's floor quad is collapsed to a degenerate point. The existing wall geometry already shows the cut interior; the new per-cell floor just makes the underside disappear for cut-through cells.

## Phases

### Phase 1 — Geometry restructure (~1 d)
- New FLOOR_PER_CELL_BASE region: append 4×N verts to the static buffer; indices = 6×N triangles. Pre-fill XY corners statically, Z starts at floorZ - 0.05.
- Drop the single FLOOR_BASE quad (4 verts + 6 indices).
- Two-material split (extends k94n's existing split): main material for cells + walls + fringes; floor material for per-cell floors. geometry.addGroup ranges updated.
- TOTAL_VERTS += 4·N - 4; index buffer += 6·N - 6.

### Phase 2 — Update path (~0.5 d)
- New helper writeCellFloor(ix, iy, z): if z ≤ floorZ + ε collapse all four verts to one cell-center point at floorZ (degenerate triangles drop in rasterizer); else restore the four corners.
- Wire into updateHeights right after writeTop.
- Dirty-AABB upload range widens to cover the per-cell floor region for the affected cells.

### Phase 3 — LOD pyramid (~0.5 d)
- Each pyramid level builds its own per-cell floors. Min-pooled values already determine cut-through correctly (MIN of a pool block at floorZ collapses that block's floor).
- setActiveLevel's full re-pool already drives the write path.

### Phase 4 — Tests + cleanup (~0.5 d)
- Unit test: construct mesh, set one cell to floorZ, assert that cell's floor quad collapses and neighbour's stays.
- Drop the now-unnecessary 0.05 mm offset on non-cut floors.

## Risks

- **Memory**: +48 MB at 1M cells (positions + normals + indices). LOD minLevel clamp keeps L0 from being active on heavy stocks, so practical worst case is similar to today.
- **Edge-overlay rebuild**: +33% triangles. The 400k-tri cap already gates this.
- **Dirty-AABB calc**: must include the per-cell floor verts in the upload range. Off-by-one is the main risk.

## Acceptance

- Top view of cut-through cells: unchanged.
- Bottom view of cut-through cells: empty space (the goal).
- 60 fps at 1M-cell test corpus.
- Backward scrub still clears cut-through floor collapse.
close_reason: Closed

title: Toolset + machine save/load files; machine name + capabilities; merge on project open

title: Tool library × op constraints audit + UX gaps
description:
Per the user's review of the tool library against Estlcam.

Findings:

1. Per-op tool-kind constraints exist only for V-Carve (VCarveSection) and Chamfer (ChamferSection) — both show a 'Tool kind mismatch — needs a V-bit' chip. Profile / Pocket / Drill / Engrave / Drag-knife do NOT validate. A user can assign a drill bit to a Profile op and silently get nonsense gcode. Mirror the chip pattern in the remaining sections.

2. dragoff (drag-knife pivot offset) is buried in the expanded section. For drag_knife it's the SINGLE most important field — surface it in the main tool row.

3. zShiftMm (per-tool Z stickout offset) is the field that lands the cutting tip at the right Z (rt1.30). Today it's only in the expanded section. Surface it in the main row + clarify the label ('Tool length offset (mm)' or similar).

4. Tool overall length: Estlcam doesn't expose a separate field — H_Cut (flute length) + Z_Shift cover the use cases (engagement model + tip-Z compensation). We already have both (fluteLengthMm, zShiftMm). No new field needed; just surface them.

5. Mesh stickout: today buildEndmillStack and the drill mesh use diameter-multiplied defaults. fluteLengthMm already overrides for endmill; the drill mesh currently picks max(d*6, 8) regardless. Plumb fluteLengthMm through the drill mesh too.

Acceptance:
- Each opKind has a clear allowed-tool-kinds set, and OpPropertiesPanel shows a 'Tool kind mismatch' chip when the bound tool doesn't fit.
- dragoff visible in the main tool row when kind === 'drag_knife'.
- zShiftMm visible in the main tool row regardless of kind (it's the universal tip-Z field).
- Drill 3D mesh respects fluteLengthMm.
close_reason: Closed

title: Tool fields + 3D mesh per kind: drill flutes/angle, drill body+tip mesh
description:
Per-tool-kind audit of which fields apply, plus the 3D preview shape.

Today the tool library DISABLES flutes and tipAngleDeg for drill ('Flutes not used for drill', 'Tip angle only applies to V-bits / engravers'). That's wrong: twist drills have flutes (typically 2) and a tip angle (typically 118°). Estlcam exposes both for Bohrer-type tools (see _TP.Flutes, _TP.Angle in the decompile).

Today the drill 3D-preview mesh is a tapered cone with the apex at the cutting tip — drills are cylindrical bodies with a short 118° conical tip, not a slim full-body cone like a V-bit.

Fixes:
1. fieldApplies('flutes', 'drill') → true; default 2 on kind change.
2. fieldApplies('tipAngleDeg', 'drill') → true; default 118 on kind change.
3. tool_mesh.ts drill branch: cylinder body + conical tip whose apex angle = tipAngleDeg.
4. Update the tooltip text in fieldReasonForKind so it doesn't claim drill has no flutes / tip angle.
close_reason: Closed

title: Pre-select best-fit tool when adding an op against a selection
description: When adding a new op with a selected object, pre-pick the tool from the library that best matches the geometry. For Drill: if the selected object has length≈width (square / circle within a tolerance), pick the tool whose diameter is closest to length. Tie-break order: exact ≤ tolerance → next smallest diameter → next largest. For other op kinds, similar heuristics (Profile = tool ≤ smallest pocket gap, etc.) — start with Drill since the geometry signal is unambiguous.

title: Status bar: show selection center + L×W instead of bbox/segs/unit_scale
description: The bottom status bar currently reads e.g. 'bbox=(5.76,5.79)–(24.22,24.24) · 4096 segments · unit_scale=1'. None of that is actionable while editing. title: V-Carve perimeter-only mode (Estlcam-style for wide regions)
description:
When a V-Carve op targets a closed region wider than 2×max_carve_width, today's medial-axis traversal cuts a spine pattern through the interior. Estlcam's V-Carve only traces the BOUNDARY offset inward by max_width/2, leaving the centre plateau untouched (see c_Carve.cs analysis, 2026-05-20).

Both behaviours produce identical results on text / narrow contours (the dominant V-Carve use case). They diverge for any single deliberately-wide region — e.g. a heart-shaped pocket with a V-carved rim. Estlcam users coming to wiac expect the rim-only result.

## Implementation

- Add 'perimeter_only: bool' (default false) to VCarveParams.
- When set, the op driver bypasses medial_axis_cached and instead:
  - For each region, compute parallel_offset_inward(boundary, R) where R = effective_r_cap (= min(carve_max_width/2, tool_reach_r/2 actually tool_reach itself)) — re-use the existing cavalier_contours/clipper2 offset primitive that Profile / Pocket-cascade already share.
  - Emit each offset polyline at constant z = -R/tan(angle/2), no ratchet (perimeter is flat).
- Frontend: VCarveSection adds a checkbox 'Perimeter only (Estlcam style)'.
- Test: 30×30 square with perimeter_only emits a single boundary-offset loop, not the medial-axis cross.

## Why P3, not P4

Real user expectation gap vs Estlcam — wide-region V-carve is a documented use case and the current spine pattern produces extra cuts that look wrong. Small surface area (~50 LOC + tests).

## Names considered
- perimeter_only (clearest)
- estlcam_style (vague)
- skip_interior (negative phrasing)
First wins.

LABELS: cam, vcarve, estlcam-merge
close_reason: Closed

title: bww: object_meta[].bbox not transformed by applyFileTransform
description:
applyFileTransform (file-transform.ts:33-45) only rewrites segments and bbox of the import. object_meta[].bbox values stay in original (untransformed) coordinates.

## Symptoms
- PatternSection's 'Set polar center from selection' button computes a center from object_meta[i].bbox — when a fileTransform is applied (translate / scale / rotate) the resulting center lands at the ORIGINAL drawing location, not where the user sees the geometry on the canvas.
- Latent — exposed today via wrsu Phase 5a (transformedImport reads object_meta) but pre-existed: it already broke single-import + transform users.

## Fix
applyFileTransform should also map object_meta[i].bbox through the same affine, or compute it by walking the transformed segments belonging to that id. The latter is more robust (rotation doesn't preserve axis-aligned bbox extents).
close_reason: Closed

title: wrsu Phase 5b: drop proxy accessors + collapse legacy bww plumbing
description:
Phase 5a migrated external consumers; Phase 5b removes the shim now that no external read targets it.

## Scope
- Drop ProjectState.imported / fileTransform / lastImportPath proxy getter/setters (lines ~219-257, ~512-518 in state/project.svelte.ts).
- Drop CommandTarget.imported and .fileTransform fields (commands.ts:47-48).
- Drop legacy patchFileTransform / resetFileTransform / setFileTransformCommand / replaceImportedCommand / appendImportedCommand. The per-import variants (patchFileTransformForImport / resetFileTransformForImport / setImportsCommand) replace them.
- Rewrite internal class methods that wrote to this.imported (setImported, appendImportedSegments, deleteLayer, snapshot/restore) to operate on this.data.imports[] directly. Each gets an explicit ImportEntry shape.
- The legacy single-import undoable wrappers go through setImportsCommand with a 1-entry array swap.

## Why
The shim was carrying its weight during the multi-file rollout; once Phase 5a removed every external dependency it's now dead surface area that confuses junior devs reading the project state (two ways to do the same thing).

## Risk
Higher than 5a — touches setImported() (project boundary), snapshot/restore (project file persistence), and the appendImportedSegments path used by Add Text. All have unit tests but no integration tests. Worth a manual AppImage smoke test after.

title: 6y3m follow-up: text width % scaling (50–200 %, TextLayer.widthScale)

Part 2 of the original 6y3m bd. Add a 'Width' percent slider (50–200 %, default 100 %) to AddTextDialog + TextList edit panel that scales the rendered text horizontally without changing height.

## Surface

title: Perf jzpl Phase 2 follow-up: intern layer names in DXF / SVG importers
description:
Phase 2 changed Segment.layer + VcObject.layer to Arc<str>. The CLONE path is now alloc-free for the layer field. The CONSTRUCTION path (DXF / SVG / text importers) still allocates a fresh Arc<str> per Segment because each Segment::line call does `Arc::from(&str)` internally.

## Fix
- Add a small LayerIntern helper: `struct LayerIntern { map: HashMap<String, Arc<str>> }` with `intern(&mut self, name: &str) -> Arc<str>`.
- Plumb through ImportCtx (dxf_in.rs) and the SVG / text importers.
- Each layer string is allocated ONCE per import; all segments on the same layer share the Arc.

## Why
For a 5000-segment DXF with 4 layer names, peak heap drops from 5000 Arc<str> allocations to 4. Doesn't change clone performance (already cheap) but reduces import-time alloc churn.
close_reason: Closed

title: Perf jzpl Phase 3: lazy pattern emission (Drill-only fast path)
description:
Pattern expansion at offset_builder.rs:103-139 materializes N×K VcObjects per pattern op (10×10 grid × 100 selected = 10000 clones). After kbx5 patterns are Drill-only, so each clone is a tiny 1-segment marker.

## Fix
- Stop materializing pattern instances. `pattern_offsets()` already returns the instance list; refactor build_op_offsets to compute the OFFSET set once on source objects, then iterate instances at emit time applying `apply_pattern_to_point` to the offset polyline.
- Drill driver (the only kind with patterns post-kbx5): drill markers reduce to (x, y) — a 2-float transform per instance.
- Containment / cascade: drills don't cascade, so no graph rebuild needed. Future kinds (when they get pattern support back) need more care.

## Why
For a 100-hole × 10×10 drill plate: 10000 VcObject clones → 100 offset computations + 100 transformed-emit loops.

NOTE: After Phase 2 (Arc<str> for layer), the VcObject clone cost drops dramatically (the layer String was the dominant heap cost). Benchmark before/after Phase 2 to decide whether Phase 3 is still worth the refactor. ~400 LOC, touches drill emit loop.

title: Feat: multi-file imports — place multiple drawings on the same stock
description:
Multi-file imports — place several drawings on the same stock. The bww (file transform) gave layout control for ONE drawing; this completes the use case.

## Phased plan (each phase is its own commit/PR)

### Phase 1: state shape + persistence (BACKWARD-COMPAT, zero behavior change)
- ProjectDataState.imports: ImportEntry[] where ImportEntry = { id, source: ImportResponse, fileTransform: FileTransform, lastImportPath? }
- Keep imported / fileTransform / lastImportPath / transformedImport as derived backward-compat getters that target imports[0].
- ProjectFile gains imports field; on load, old files with bare 'imported' field are migrated into a single-entry imports array.
- Commands' CommandTarget shape gains imports[]; mutations route through it.
- All 64+ consumers of project.imported keep working unchanged.

### Phase 2: per-import file ops + UI
- loadFile / openFile add a new ImportEntry (vs replace).
- 'Replace' vs 'Add' affordance in LayerList header.
- File transform UI moves into a per-import section in LayerList.
- 'Remove this import' action per entry.

### Phase 3: canvas rendering for N imports
- EntityCanvas2D iterates all imports.
- transformedImport derived returns combined view (or per-import).
- Hit-test resolves to (importId, segIdx, objectId).
- Selection by (importId, objectId) tuple; object-id namespacing avoided by carrying importId everywhere.

### Phase 4: pipeline payload
- Ops gain importId field.
- build-project sends all imports' segments concatenated.
- Op resolution uses (importId, objectId) tuples; pipeline cache key namespaces accordingly.

### Phase 5: cleanup
- Drop the imported shim.
- All consumers read imports directly.
- bww's fileTransform plumbing collapses since each ImportEntry owns its own.

## Why phased
N=many consumers (64+ project.imported reads). A big-bang would touch everything at once. With backward-compat shims at Phase 1, each subsequent phase migrates one slice independently and can ship by itself.
close_reason: Closed

title: UX: auto-regenerate G-code on edit (debounced, opt-in setting)

title: UX audit pass: status-bar hints + tooltip coverage on weak dialogs
description:
User requested an under-covered UX pass: tooltips on tools/settings + status-bar reminders for modal states (ESC to finish, right click, CTRL+click for multi-select, etc.).

Work completed:
- App.svelte: centralized status-bar hint in a derived (modalStatusHint > statusInfoText + statusShortcutHints). Covers approach-pick mode (existing), tab-placement mode (new — manual/mixed Profile/Pocket ops), and idle/selection shortcut tail (Shift/Ctrl/right-click/?). Footer-pick accent class drives on any modal hint.
- AddTextDialog.svelte: tooltips on text, font-bundled / font-custom radios, size, position X/Y, tool, depth (1 → 8).
- MachineDialog.svelte: tooltips on unit, mode, fast-move Z, comments, arcs, supportsToolchange, rapid speed, tool-change time, jerk-enable (6 → 13).

title: audit 2026-05-17: extract EntityCanvas2D selection reducer + box-select threshold
description:
